analysis.one_liner: Makes drugmakers pay Medicare rebates when prices outpace inflation and caps seniors' out-of-pocket drug costs.
analysis.headline: The Senate Finance chairman's drug pricing bill, introduced July 2, 2020 with 10 Republican cosponsors, sat in committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets prescription drug prices in Medicare and Medicaid. It requires drugmakers to pay rebates to Medicare when a drug's price rises faster than inflation, and to refund Medicare for the discarded portion of single-dose vials. It rewrites the Medicare Part D drug benefit so seniors pay lower coinsurance, face a lower out-of-pocket threshold, and owe nothing in cost-sharing above it, with brand-name drugmakers partly financing that through mandatory discounts. It also forces pharmacy benefit managers to disclose their rebates and bans them from keeping a hidden markup in Medicaid.
analysis.who_benefits: Seniors on Medicare, who would pay lower coinsurance (cut from 25% to 20% above the deductible), hit a lower out-of-pocket threshold ($3,100 in 2023), and owe no cost-sharing above it. Medicaid programs and taxpayers, who benefit from higher manufacturer rebates, an end to 'spread pricing' where a middleman pockets the difference between what it charges the state and pays the pharmacy, and refunds for discarded drug amounts. People with private insurance gain indirectly from price pressure and public disclosure of rebate flows.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors on Medicare and Medicaid patients

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate for Part B and Part D drugs whose prices rise faster than inflation, measured from a mid-2019 baseline, with refunds deposited into the Medicare trust fund.

Lowers the Medicare Part D out-of-pocket threshold (set at $3,100 for 2023) and eliminates beneficiary cost-sharing entirely above that threshold, and cuts coinsurance above the deductible from 25% to 20% starting in 2023.
Requires manufacturers to refund Medicare for the amount of single-dose vial drugs that providers must discard, ending a billing practice where patients and taxpayers paid for unused medicine.

Requires public disclosure of pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) discounts and rebates, and prohibits spread pricing in Medicaid, requiring pass-through pricing so states and pharmacies see the real prices.
Increases the maximum rebate drugmakers owe under the Medicaid Drug Rebate Program and applies Medicaid rebate requirements to drugs provided in outpatient hospital settings.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers bear the direct cost: inflation rebates, discarded-drug refunds, deeper Medicaid rebates, and mandatory discounts that partly fund the richer Part D benefit. Pharmacy benefit managers lose an opaque revenue stream. Some of the drug-benefit redesign shifts cost dynamics between plans, manufacturers, and premiums, and Medicare pays more for biosimilar competitors in the short term.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drugmakers and pharmacy benefit managers

drawbacks.text: The bill does not let the government negotiate or cap launch prices for new drugs; it only rebates price increases above inflation after the fact, so manufacturers keep full pricing power over what a new drug costs when it launches.

A manufacturer can terminate its discount-program agreement 'for any reason' with roughly a year's notice, so the financing behind the richer drug benefit depends on voluntary continued participation rather than an enforceable long-term commitment.

The bill temporarily increases Medicare payments for biosimilar copies (an 8% add-on) to encourage competition, which raises federal spending in the short run in hopes of building a market for cheaper copies.
Much of the bill is disclosure rather than price control: study-and-report provisions and public dashboards aim at accountability but do not directly lower any price by themselves.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core provisions are real: inflation rebates, the out-of-pocket cap, and the discarded-drug refund put costs on an industry whose prices had long outpaced inflation, and they deliver concrete relief to seniors. The honest limits are that the bill leaves launch pricing untouched, leans on manufacturer discounts that firms can walk away from, and spends public money to seed biosimilar competition. On balance it is a substantial, if incremental, benefit to patients financed largely by drugmakers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee on July 2, 2020, and nothing further happened before that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA) introduced the Prescription Drug Pricing Reduction Act of 2020 on July 2, 2020, joined by 10 Republican cosponsors.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance, the only committee action ever taken on it.
The bill never received a committee vote, a floor vote, or House action, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers are better off, because the rebates, refunds, and transparency requirements never took effect. Seniors gained nothing, though the same ideas later resurfaced in other drug pricing legislation.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Drug manufacturers and pharmacy benefit managers

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-IA), Chairman of the Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, which would have imposed inflation rebates on drugmakers and redesigned the Part D benefit.

for.name: 10 Senate Republicans
for.role: Cosponsors including Portman, Cassidy, Collins, Ernst, and Murkowski
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill or comparable Senate drug pricing legislation for a floor vote in the 116th Congress, despite Grassley's public push for floor time.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry (PhRMA and major manufacturers)
against.role: Trade association and its member drug companies
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against Senate drug pricing legislation including inflation rebates and helped keep similar proposals from reaching the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat signed on, but the bill drew no recorded vote, so the actual partisan split never showed up on the floor.

industries.note: The bill takes money directly from these manufacturers through inflation-based Medicare rebates, refunds for discarded single-dose vials, a higher Medicaid rebate cap, and mandatory discounts that partly fund seniors' lower out-of-pocket costs. Their gain under the status quo is ordinary people's higher drug bills, so their interest in blocking it runs against the public.

The bill forces PBMs to publicly disclose the rebates and fees they take and bans spread pricing in Medicaid, eliminating a practice where the middleman pockets the gap between what states pay and what pharmacies receive. Their hidden margin comes at the cost of taxpayers and pharmacies.
The bill temporarily raises Medicare payment for biosimilar copies of expensive biologics to build market share for cheaper alternatives, which would eventually lower costs for patients.

Banning Medicaid spread pricing and requiring PBM price concessions to reach the point of sale means pharmacies are paid closer to the actual negotiated price, ending a practice that squeezed them and inflated state costs.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D plans and insurers
industries.note: Plans lose revenue from the larger manufacturer discounts and the shrinking reinsurance share, but those same discounts count toward their bids and must reach beneficiaries at the pharmacy counter, largely offsetting the hit while adding compliance burdens.
